newsitem.title: UK: UK stock market, near record, seen lagging Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK stock market, near record, seen lagging Europe.

text.p: British stocks have underperformed most European bourses this year and will stay near the bottom of the pack if the continent's record run continues, strategists said on Tuesday.

Even though analysts seem convinced the FTSE 100 index of Britain's top companies will hit the 5,000 point barrier, rising UK interest rates and a very strong sterling will keep the London market behind the rest of Europe's top performing markets.
The leading UK blue chip index, which has risen 20 percent so far this year, was up 62 points at 1540 GMT Tuesday at 4,957.9. Its lifetime high is 4,998.1.

"We will almost certainly see 5,000 points but we will also see smaller percentage gains than in many continental markets, like Germany, Amsterdam, Switzerland, Spain and Italy," said Roger Monson, chief equity strategist at Daiwa Europe.
His year-end target for the FTSE 100 is 5,200, up about six percent from Monday's close, while other European markets should gain at least 10 percent.
The current year price/earnings ratio for the UK is 16, versus the typical continental market of 19 to 22, Monson said. "It is cheaper but it has these obstacles to contend with," he said.
In the first six months of 1997, the UK market rose 12 percent, versus 43 percent in Switzerland, 33 percent Netherlands, 30 percent Germany and 25 percent Italy, he said.
Higher interest rates increase the cost of borrowing, make fixed-income investments more attractive and can slow down the economy, hitting profits.
UK interest rates have been hiked three times in the last three months and a fourth rate increase, to 7.0 percent, is expected by the newly-independent Bank of England this week.
A Reuters poll of economists showed 16 of 23 expected a 25 basis point hike after the Bank's monetary policy committee (MPC) meets on Wednesday and Thursday.
The spectre of further rate increases later this year, to dampen buoyant consumer spending, would cast a black cloud over the equity market.

"Given that the interest rate cycle in the UK is less supportive than the rest of Europe, those other markets may continue to enjoy a lower interest rate environment, even though we have underperformed," said Corey Miller, equities strategist at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
The other edge of the sword, however, is the strength of sterling as it stays perched above three German marks.
Strong sterling, which edged back up toward its decade-high peak against the mark, hits companies when they exchange profits back into sterling and hamstrings their competitiveness.

Spotlighting that concern was a warning from British Airways Plc on Monday that its earnings were getting hammered by the sterling's rise. Profits in the three months to the end of June were cut by 77 million pounds due to sterling, it said.
Big-cap engineering companies, like GKN Plc, which reports half-year results on Wednesday, are seen especially vulnerable.
"The strength of sterling is still not reflected in earnings expectations," said Mike Young, director of European investment strategy at Goldman Sachs.

The UK is probably the cheapest major market in Europe, he said, but a "visible peaking of sterling against the continental currencies" is needed before the FTSE 100 starts to outperform. That probably will not happen until later this year, he said.

"We think we will see continued underperformance (in the UK market) on a three-month horizon," he said. "This is clearly the economy in Europe where interest rates are being raised and we don't believe the necessary increases are fully discounted by the market."
